title: Frogging
subtitle: Pulling out rows of crochet and starting a section again
excerpt: Frogging means unravelling a section of crochet by pulling the working yarn. Named for the 'rip it, rip it' sound. Faster than tinking but uncontrolled — you pull back to before the problem and re-work from there. The trick is stopping at the right row.
sourceNotes: Standard crochet craft terminology. Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book.

glossaryTerms.definition: Unravelling crochet by pulling the working yarn, removing multiple rows or rounds at once. From 'rip it, rip it'. Faster than tinking but requires re-picking up the live loop from a previous row.
The working loop currently on the hook, or the loop at the end of the last completed stitch after frogging — the point where work can resume.

heroPrompt: A crochet swatch in DK cotton mid-frog — several rows of yarn pulled out and sitting loose, with the live loop held on the hook at the row where the frog stopped.

content.text: The word 'frogging' is crafter slang: because you 'rip it, rip it, rip it'. Pulling the working yarn unravels the stitches back through whatever rows you want to remove. Faster than tinking (stitch-by-stitch) and the right tool when you need to go back more than a few stitches — but it needs a controlled stop to avoid unravelling past the target row.
How to frog without losing your place
Identify the row you want to return to — the last correct row before the mistake.
Remove the hook from the working loop and gently pull the working yarn to unravel the rows above the target.
Stop ONE ROW above the target row. The

should be at the start of the row you want to remove. Insert the hook carefully into each stitch of this row one at a time, pulling gently to release the remaining row. This controlled unravelling prevents overshooting.
Once back to the last correct row, re-insert the hook under the last stitch loop of that row and resume work.
When frogging is the right call
A mistake more than 5-6 stitches back in the current row, or in a previous row.
A pattern error discovered 2+ rows after it occurred.
Gauge or sizing problems discovered early enough that reworking is faster than finishing and seaming a piece that won't fit.

attrs.title: Yarn gets fuzzy from frogging
attrs.body: Wool and mohair develop a halo from repeated working and unravelling — the fibres loosen and stick to themselves. If you are working with a fuzzy yarn, frogging back more than a few times can make the yarn too fluffy to re-work cleanly. Cotton and smooth acrylic recover better.
